analysis.one_liner: Caps the total cost of federal regulation and lets the White House budget office block enforcement of rules over the cap.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2016 with two cosponsors, the bill never left the Senate Homeland Security Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat federal regulation like federal spending: each year's budget would set a dollar cap on the total cost that businesses, states, and local governments incur complying with federal rules, divided among committees and agencies. Any rule that pushed compliance costs over the cap could be barred from enforcement, and private lawsuits could challenge enforcement. It would also require detailed cost estimates for new rules and full public comment for major agency guidance documents.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries facing federal compliance costs would gain a hard cap on the total regulatory burden, a White House office empowered to block enforcement of rules over the cap, and a new court claim against enforcement. Small businesses would gain extra analysis of their compliance costs.

how_it_helps.text: The annual budget resolution would have to set a cap on total federal regulatory compliance cost for at least five years, allocated among committees, agencies, and programs.
Agencies would have to provide detailed estimates of private-sector compliance costs for major rules, including how costs fall on small businesses and other businesses, and only in numerical form.
Significant guidance documents — those with roughly $100 million or more in annual effects — could not be issued without notice and an opportunity for public comment.

Points of order would block legislation exceeding regulatory allocations unless 60 percent of members voted to waive, and a private right of action would let regulated parties sue over enforcement of over-cap rules or un-noticed guidance.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, workers, patients, and communities who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial rules: the cap counts compliance costs but excludes the value of benefits, so over time new protections could be blocked or go unenforced. Agencies would also lose the ability to issue timely guidance.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The cap counts all compliance costs incurred by the private sector, states, and local governments but explicitly excludes the value of any benefit the rule produces, so the arithmetic is rigged against regulation by design.

OMB could issue a directive prohibiting agencies from spending funds to enforce any rule it determines would breach the cap — letting an unelected office stop enforcement of rules Congress or agencies adopted.

The definition of federal regulatory cost includes the cost of complying with any federal statute, not just new rules, which makes the cap effectively unmeetable and would force cuts to enforcement of existing law.
A private right of action would invite litigation against enforcement of over-cap rules and agency guidance that skipped notice and comment, further slowing regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency pieces — better cost estimates, CBO look-back reviews comparing estimates to actual costs — are modest and useful on their own. But the core enforcement machinery is built to shrink regulation regardless of what rules achieve: costs are counted, benefits are excluded, and one White House office could unilaterally stop enforcement. The cost in delayed or abandoned health, safety, environmental, and financial protections would far outweigh the bookkeeping benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in May 2016, the committee never acted on it, and the 114th Congress ended without the bill ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on May 25, 2016 with Sens. Rubio and Enzi; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no report, no vote — and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 without the bill receiving floor consideration.
The bill's cap would have counted only compliance costs and excluded benefits, and OMB could have barred enforcement of rules exceeding the cap.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial rules: the existing rulemaking process stayed intact, and regulated industries did not get the compliance-cost cap they would have gained.

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Article I Regulatory Budget Act on May 25, 2016.

for.role: U.S. Senator, cosponsor (Chair, Senate Budget Committee)

against.name: Ron Johnson

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill after it was referred; the committee took no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it remained in committee through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and the bill drew no Democratic support; no recorded votes were ever taken, so the split was never tested.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, chemical, and financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would cap total compliance costs — counting costs but excluding benefits — and let OMB block enforcement of rules over the cap, plus open a court route to challenge enforcement. The industry's gain in lower compliance costs is the public's loss of new health, safety, environmental, and financial protections.

Amendments to the Regulatory Flexibility Act would require agencies to detail compliance costs on small entities and analyze alternatives. Small firms would share in reduced regulatory burden but also in the loss of protections the rules provide.
